title: This Is Your Victory, O Lord
story:
Karna had stripped Bhima of his chariot, and the taunts were still ringing in his ears. Standing on the bare ground with his bow in his hand, Bhima shouted across the din to Arjuna: Karna had called him eunuch, fool, glutton, unskilled in weapons, and had done it in Arjuna's very sight. "You know the vow I made along with you," he cried. "Remember the words I spoke then. Do not let my vow, or yours, be falsified. Do what will make my vow true."

To be made carless was to be left standing on the open field, horses and driver gone, an easy mark for the next charge. And this was a day already heavy with vows. That morning Arjuna had sworn to slay Jayadratha — who had helped cut his son Abhimanyu down — before the sun set. That vow was spent: Jayadratha lay dead, and Vriddhakshatra, his father, had died with him. But now a second oath hung in the air.

Arjuna rode up to Karna, and his words came cold and exact. "You fight falsely," he said, "and you applaud yourself. A hero meets one of two things in battle, victory or defeat, and both are uncertain even when Indra himself fights. When Yuyudhana made you carless, your senses left you and you stood at the very point of death. Remembering the vow I had made to slay you, that hero dismissed you without taking your life. The truly righteous, having vanquished a foe, never boast and never speak ill of anyone. You did deprive Bhima of his car, it is true; but your abuse of him was sinful. Since you have spoken so harshly of him, and since you with others slew the son of Subhadra out of my sight, you shall reap the fruit of it this very day. I will slay Vrishasena before your eyes, and every king who advances against me I will send to Yama's abode. Accomplish now whatever you must, for a great calamity is hanging over you."

A loud and tremendous uproar rose among the car-warriors at those words. And at that frightful time, when confusion was everywhere, the thousand-rayed sun dimmed its rays and went down behind the Asta hill.

Then Krishna, stationed in the van of battle, took Arjuna in his arms. "By good luck, your great vow is accomplished," he said. "By good luck, Vriddhakshatra is slain along with his son. Even the commander of the celestial army, meeting this host of Dhritarashtra's, would lose his senses in battle — there is no doubt of it. Except you, I do not see in all the three worlds the man who could fight this force. Many royal warriors equal to you, or greater, have joined together at Duryodhana's command; clad in mail, they could not come near you, meeting your angry self in battle. Your energy and your might are equal to Rudra's, to the Destroyer's own. None else could put forth such prowess as you, alone and unsupported, put forth today. And I shall applaud you again, in the same words, when Karna of wicked soul is slain along with his followers; I shall glorify you when that enemy of yours lies vanquished."

Arjuna answered with a humility the field had seldom seen from him. "Through your grace," he said, "this vow, which even the gods could accomplish only with difficulty, has been accomplished by me. It is no wonder that those who have you for their lord win. Through your grace, Yudhishthira will obtain the whole earth. All this is your power. This is your victory, my lord. Our prosperity is your victory."

The two stood together in the van while the last light drained out of the sky — the warrior who had kept his word, and the friend who had driven him to it. The vow was spent, and the day was done. In the dark that was gathering, the war would go on.
reflection: Arjuna's answer is the heart of the scene: at the peak of his powers, having done what even the gods found difficult, he gives the victory entirely to Krishna. The praise never reaches his head because he understands the deed as Krishna's — devotion carried by an act, not by adjectives.
next_story_tease: As the chariot bore them back across the field, Krishna turned Arjuna's gaze to what his shafts had left behind.
hero_scene: At sunset on the battlefield, Krishna embraces Arjuna in the van of the army, one hand on his shoulder, as the last light drains behind the Asta hill and the banners stir in the dusk.
